summary: Discusses the design thinking behind the iSCSI session model and how it relates to SCSI command ordering. An iSCSI session matches the SCSI I_T nexus and gives ordered command delivery from initiator to target. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Commands to a disk must arrive in the right order. This explains why iSCSI was built so they do.

questions: how does iscsi keep scsi commands in order
subtitle: Why an iSCSI session guarantees that SCSI commands reach the target in order, and how to build on that.

tldr.problem: Storage applications such as remote mirroring and tape vaulting stream many SCSI commands back to back over long-delay networks, and some of them break if the commands execute out of order.
tldr.mechanism: An iSCSI session maps to the SCSI I_T nexus, and the target iSCSI layer reorders commands by Command Sequence Number (CmdSN) so the SCSI layer sees one ordered flow, even across several TCP connections and even after errors.
tldr.outcome: Designers can treat ordered command delivery as a built-in property of iSCSI and layer SCSI features such as ORDERED task attributes, ACA or UA interlock on top of it. The RFC is informational and adds no new protocol rules.

facts.label: SCSI task attributes
facts.value: SIMPLE, ORDERED, HEAD OF QUEUE, ACA

today: RFC 3783 is an Informational RFC and no obsoleting or updating RFC is recorded for it. It explains the design intent of the iSCSI specification, RFC 3720, rather than defining new protocol rules.

sections.title: Why Command Ordering Matters
sections.content:
iSCSI carries SCSI over TCP/IP, so an initiator and a target can be very far apart. The RFC lists larger storage area networks, asynchronous remote mirroring and remote tape vaulting as new uses. Because of the long delays, an initiator has a strong incentive to stream commands back to back without waiting for the status of earlier ones.

Some applications do not care about the execution order. Others do. A mirroring application does not want writes committed out of order on the remote target, because that would damage the transactional integrity of the data there. Streaming plus guaranteed ordered execution is therefore valuable for a critical class of applications.
sections.eli5: If you are copying a diary to a faraway friend, the pages must be written in order or the story makes no sense. Sending many pages at once is fast, but only if they stay in order.

sections.title: The Session as an I_T Nexus
sections.content:
In SCSI, the I_T nexus is the relationship between an initiator port and a target port. iSCSI represents it as a session, which may span one or more TCP connections (as many as 216). The SCSI layer sees only one logical flow, even in a multi-connection session. A session is identified by a session identifier made of an Initiator Session Identifier (ISID) and a Target Session Identifying Handle (TSIH), and each connection has a connection identifier (CID).

Four features together hide the multiple connections from SCSI:

  • Ordered command delivery: commands striped across connections are reordered by the target using the session-wide Command Sequence Number (CmdSN).
  • Connection allegiance: all PDUs for one command, up to and including its SCSI Response PDU, flow on the same connection at a given time.
  • Task set management handling: for ABORT TASK SET and CLEAR TASK SET, the initiator receives the responses of unaffected tasks before the TMF response.
  • Immediate TMF handling: an immediate task management request acts as if commands and the request travelled on a single logical channel.
sections.eli5: A session is like one phone call that secretly uses several phone lines. The listener hears one steady conversation and never knows several lines were used.

sections.title: The Ordering Guarantee and Who Owns It
sections.content:
Two design questions came up early: what ordering behaviour is needed when transport errors occur, and whether both initiators and targets must use ordered delivery. For the first, RFC 3347 concluded that iSCSI must specify strictly ordered delivery of SCSI commands over a session, even in the presence of transport errors. A digest failure or a connection termination must not let the target execute commands in an order different from the CmdSN order.

For the second, the answer was that initiators need not always use ordering. The onus of ensuring ordered delivery is always on the target, which simply always provides the service. It is the initiator's discretion whether to rely on it. The guarantee covers the whole I_T nexus, across all the logical units the nexus may access.

Because ordering across connections is what a multi-connection session is for, the RFC advises that where this cross-connection ordering is judged expensive, several single-connection sessions should be considered instead.
sections.eli5: The post office (the target) always sorts your letters by number. Whether you care about the order is up to you, but the sorting is always done.

sections.title: SCSI Tools That Build on Ordered Delivery
sections.content:
The SCSI layer has several features for enforcing ordering. All of them assume the transport delivers commands in order, which is the missing piece iSCSI supplies.

  • Command Reference Number (CRN): a sequence number per I_T_L nexus. There is no SCSI-generic way to enable it, and iSCSI chose not to support it.
  • Task attributes: SIMPLE, ORDERED, HEAD OF QUEUE and ACA. Careful use of ORDERED and SIMPLE on a pipelined stream can convey the exact execution schema, provided commands arrive in the same order.
  • Auto Contingent Allegiance (ACA): triggered when a command with the NACA bit set completes with CHECK CONDITION. It blocks all commands except those with the ACA attribute until CLEAR ACA is executed.
  • UA interlock: keeps a Unit Attention condition until the same initiator runs an explicit REQUEST SENSE. It also covers BUSY, TASK SET FULL and RESERVATION CONFLICT statuses, and was created to get ordering without the side effects of the TST bit.
sections.eli5: SCSI gives you tools like a red flag that stops the line when something goes wrong. These tools only work well if the items on the conveyor belt arrive in order, and iSCSI makes sure of that.

sections.title: Connection Failures and Design Guidance
sections.content:
When a connection fails, iSCSI requires active tasks on it to be terminated if not recovered within a negotiated time limit. The danger is that the target's SCSI layer would move on and run later tasks out of order without the initiator knowing. To prevent that, iSCSI mandates two things. First, the terminated tasks are treated internally as if they ended with CHECK CONDITION, which triggers ACA if the initiator uses it. Second, the target must report a Unit Attention on the next command for each affected I_T_L nexus, with CHECK CONDITION status and ASC/ASCQ 47h/7Fh (SOME COMMANDS CLEARED BY ISCSI PROTOCOL EVENT), which triggers UA interlock.

The RFC adds system considerations. Initiators should proactively avoid out-of-order situations because UA interlock is costlier when triggered. Targets that support command ordering should support command queuing, and the ORDERED and SIMPLE task attributes. Until T10 settles whether UA interlock should cover CHECK CONDITION, targets should implement both UA interlock and ACA.
sections.eli5: If a delivery truck breaks down, the post office raises an alarm so nobody thinks the missing letters were skipped on purpose.

sections.title: Reservations and Security
sections.content:
Persistent reservations are tied to SCSI initiator port names, which in iSCSI are based on ISIDs. So initiators must reuse the same ISID across sessions to different target portal groups if a reservation or registration is to work across multiple SCSI ports. To keep one across a target power loss, the initiator must use the same ISIDs as before when it re-establishes sessions after reboot.

On security, the RFC adds nothing new. It points readers to the Security Considerations of the iSCSI specification, RFC 3720.
sections.eli5: If you want the same locker every day, you have to show the same name tag every day.
